# Results — Study 158 (Super-Bowl) on the Shiller S&P 500 dataset

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Super Bowl winners and
conferences are hardcoded in [`data.py`](../super_bowl/data.py) (1967–2025, 59 games).
S&P 500 calendar-year price returns are from the Shiller monthly dataset
(`_cache/shiller_sp500.parquet`, staged in the repo-level cache). Match the
fingerprint below to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-15**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shiller S&P 500 (nominal price, December/December) | 1967–2025 | 59 years | `43c10087bc36` |
| Super Bowl table | Games I–LIX (1967–2025) | 59 games | hardcoded constant |

## The unconditional base rate — the key number

The S&P 500 rose in **43 out of 59 years** covered by our Super Bowl sample:
**unconditional up-rate = 72.9%**. This is the correct null hypothesis for
any "up/down" predictor. The common mistake in Super Bowl Indicator write-ups
is to test against a 50% coin — but the S&P is not a fair coin; it has an
upward bias that makes any "predict up" signal look prescient.

## Conference signal (NFC → bull, AFC → bear)

| Arm | n years | up-rate in group | unconditional up-rate |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| NFC wins (signal = bull) | 30 | **76.7%** | 72.9% |
| AFC wins (signal = bear) | 29 | **31.0% up** = 69.0% down | 72.9% (↓=27.1%) |

- **Overall hit-rate: 54.2%** — the signal is "correct" in 32 of 59 years.
  But the correct baseline is whether this *beats* the 72.9% unconditional
  up-rate, not a 50% coin. The NFC up-rate of 76.7% is only **+3.8pp** above
  the base rate — easily explained by 30 draws from a Bernoulli(0.729).
- **Welch t (NFC mean return vs AFC mean return): t = +0.625** — far below
  the |t| = 2 threshold. Mean NFC-year return = +10.4%, mean AFC-year = +7.8%;
  difference = 2.6pp on ~17% annual volatility with n ≈ 30 per group.
- **Binomial test** (H₀: p_up|NFC = 0.729): **p = 0.409** — not significant.
  Even if we use the lenient H₀: p = 0.5, the p-value is 0.428.
- **Permutation p-value** (shuffling conference labels 10,000 times): **p = 0.351**
  — the observed hit-rate falls comfortably inside the null distribution.

## Original-NFL signal (orig_nfl → bull)

| metric | value |
|---|--:|
| Overall hit-rate | 57.6% |
| Welch t | +1.086 |
| Binomial p (vs 72.9% base) | 0.329 |
| Permutation p | 0.248 |

Slightly stronger looking than the conference signal because the "original NFL"
category includes some AFC teams (e.g., Pittsburgh Steelers, Baltimore Colts/Ravens,
Indianapolis Colts) that happen to have won in good market years — an artifact of
which teams dominated which eras, not a predictive relationship.

## Multiple-comparisons summary (Bonferroni correction)

| Test | n | hit-rate | binom_p | perm_p | Bonferroni binom_p | Bonferroni perm_p |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| NFC win (conference) | 59 | 54.2% | 0.409 | 0.351 | 0.818 | 0.702 |
| Orig-NFL win | 59 | 57.6% | 0.329 | 0.248 | 0.658 | 0.496 |

With only 2 hypotheses, the Bonferroni adjustment barely matters — both tests
were already far from significance. The deeper problem is the tiny n.

## The n = 59 problem

With 59 total Super Bowls and ~30 per conference, and annual S&P volatility
of ~17%, the minimum detectable mean-return difference at |t| = 2 is:

    min_detectable = 17% * 2 / sqrt(30) ≈ 6.2%/yr

The observed NFC−AFC gap is only ~2.6%/yr — less than half the detectable
threshold. Even the literature's best-case years (the 1967–1997 streak where
the indicator was famously "correct") cannot survive this power calculation:
~30 years, ~17% vol, we'd need a structural 6%+ premium to detect it. There
isn't one.

## Could you trade it?

There is no tradable implementation. The signal fires once per year (or once
per Super Bowl game), in February, for a full-year calendar-year position. The
unconditional "always long S&P" benchmark already captures the 72.9% up-rate.
The indicator provides no edge over passive exposure:

- Long S&P unconditionally: 72.9% up-years, ~+9.1% mean annual return.
- Long S&P only in NFC years: 76.7% up-rate, +10.4% mean — but only 30/59 years
  in the market, missing the other 29 years with +7.8% average. The opportunity
  cost of sitting out AFC years is real.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Hit-rate 54.2%, binom p = 0.41, perm p = 0.35, Welch t = 0.63.
  No version of the Super Bowl Indicator produces a statistically significant
  signal against the correct baseline (72.9% unconditional up-rate). n = 59 is
  too small to detect anything less than a 6%/yr structural premium.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no vehicle: you can't "trade" the Super Bowl
  Indicator beyond going long or flat the S&P, which is dominated by passive buy-and-hold.
- **Busted — a coincidence dressed as an omen.** The indicator's apparent "accuracy"
  in its early years was a sampling artifact of the market's upward bias and the
  NFC's dominance during a bull market era (1967–1997). It has broken down
  repeatedly since the Patriots dynasty began in 2001.
